newsitem.title: BELGIUM: VW says more reform still needed to ensure succes.
newsitem.headline: VW says more reform still needed to ensure succes.

text.p: Volkswagen Ag, Europe's leading mass car manufacturer, said on Monday it still had much work to do if it was to succeed in an automotive industry in turmoil.

In a speech to the Automotive News Europe Congress, VW chairman Ferdinand Piech outlined VW's strategy for success, based on quality, service and price, and cutting down on the number of basic "platforms".

Common engines and components would be used in four basic platforms. But body styles would suggest many different cars. Coupes, station wagons and family saloons might be almost completely identical under the bodywork.

VW sales have powered ahead recently. Last year it increased its market share in western Europe to 17.2 per cent from the previous year's 16.8 per cent, way ahead of its nearest challenger General Motors Corp's 12.5 per cent.
In the first four months of 1997 VW market share hit 17.3 per cent. Profits have been improving, and VW is now routinely cited as analysts' favourite European automotive stock.
But Piech said much more has to be done.

"The transformation process at Volkswagen is not yet complete and will never end probably. Only some 30 percent has yet been achieved. So you can see there is still a lot to be done," Piech said in the speech.
"The automotive industry today is at a turning point," he added.

Capacity has been greater than demand, while customers' demands have increased, he said. Globalisation of markets is increasing, calling for international structures for doing business. The days are gone when profits could be generated by just raising prices.
Costs had to be constantly attacked. The "platform" strategy was the flexible vehicle to achieve this.
"In 1996 we offered our customers 38 different passenger cars. Within three years we intend to offer our customers over 50 different passenger cars," he said.
Piech said that VW's labour force had to be flexible.

"This is another key element of our current work. In order to counteract cost disadvantages in Germany it will also be necessary to treat Saturday as a normal working day not attracting exta allowances."
"The customer is not going to pay more for a car just because it was built on a Saturday," Piech said.
